title: Peripheral IV care

objectives: Describe infection-prevention practices for peripheral catheters.
Check a peripheral site daily and recognise when to remove the catheter.

items.text: Select catheters on the basis of intended purpose and duration, known complications (phlebitis, infiltration) and operator experience (CDC IB).
When therapy will likely exceed six days, a midline catheter or PICC is preferred to a short peripheral catheter (CDC Category II).
Avoid steel needles for fluids or medicines that could cause tissue necrosis if they extravasate (CDC IA).
Hand hygiene before and after palpating the site and before and after inserting, replacing, accessing, repairing or dressing a catheter (CDC IB).
Clean gloves may be used to insert a peripheral catheter if the site is not touched after skin antiseptic (CDC IC); either clean or sterile gloves when changing a dressing (CDC IC).
In adults use an upper-extremity site; move a catheter placed in a lower extremity to an upper-extremity site as soon as possible (CDC II).
Evaluate the site daily by palpation through the dressing and by inspection if the dressing is transparent; do not remove gauze or opaque dressings if there are no signs of infection (CDC II).
Who may insert, flush and remove peripheral catheters, and what may be given peripherally, is set by local policy and competence.
Catheter type, dressing and flush products follow your unit's approved supplies.
Warmth, tenderness, redness or a palpable venous cord indicate phlebitis; local tenderness or other signs may indicate infection.

Assess the site and vein at least daily, including patient-reported tenderness, and reassess when new symptoms or infusion problems arise. A clinically indicated replacement policy does not mean leaving a symptomatic catheter in use.
Insertion and flushing technique, securement and medicine compatibility: no source read supports the steps; follow the competency-approved unit procedure.

WHO 2024 allows either scheduled or clinically indicated removal of peripheral IV catheters as a conditional recommendation. Inspect the site and vein at least daily, follow the local replacement policy and arrange timely removal when no longer needed or complications arise. Preserve the separate extravasation pathway below.

For routine phlebitis, infection or malfunction, assess and arrange catheter removal under local policy. Suspected drug extravasation is a separate emergency: stop delivery through the affected site, seek immediate clinical/pharmacy assistance, and follow the drug-specific local procedure. Do not automatically remove or flush the catheter before the trained team has assessed its use in managing the injury. Arrange safe alternative access for essential therapy.
Record site checks, dressing and catheter dates, removal reasons and escalation per unit standard.

checklist.text: Perform hand hygiene before touching the site or catheter.
Palpate through the dressing (or inspect a transparent dressing) for tenderness, warmth, redness or a venous cord.
Confirm the catheter is still needed and the site is an upper-extremity site in adults.
Flush and administer using the unit's approved technique and compatibility rules.

Stop delivery through a suspected extravasation site and escalate urgently. Do not flush or automatically remove the catheter before the drug-specific local procedure is assessed; arrange safe alternative access for essential therapy.
Record the site check, dressing and catheter dates and any removal reason.

Assess the site and vein at least daily, including patient-reported tenderness, and reassess when new symptoms or infusion problems arise. A clinically indicated replacement policy does not mean leaving a symptomatic catheter in use.

gaps: Insertion technique, flushing and securement remain local. Extravasation first-response boundaries are stated; drug-specific aspiration, antidotes and catheter removal require specialist review.
